analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks through licensed gun dealers for most private firearm sales.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 46 Democratic and independent Senate cosponsors, then referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for two private individuals to transfer a firearm unless a licensed gun dealer first takes possession of it and runs a background check on the buyer, the same check that already applies at gun stores. It exempts gifts within a family, loans while hunting or at a shooting range, transfers made in self-defense emergencies, and law enforcement use. It applies to every sale, closing the private-sale loophole that now lets people buy guns from strangers without a check.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun buyers get assurance that the person they are dealing with can legally own a gun. Families and communities are protected from sales to people with felony convictions, domestic violence records, or other disqualifying histories. Licensed dealers gain a new line of business processing these transfers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun buyers and communities at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a private person to transfer a firearm unless a licensed dealer, manufacturer, or importer first takes possession of the gun to run the standard background check required of gun stores. [S2][S3]
It closes the private-sale gap: today, someone barred from owning a gun can buy one from a stranger in most states with no check at all. Under the bill, that sale must go through a dealer. [S2]

The text preserves normal life transfers: gifts between spouses, parents, children, and grandparents; loans for hunting, target shooting, or while the owner is present; transfers to prevent imminent harm; and law-enforcement and military use are all exempt. [S3]
The bill explicitly states it may not be construed to authorize a national firearms registry, and it leaves existing state gun laws in place. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Private sellers and buyers pay a dealer's fee and give up time to complete a transfer that previously took a handshake. Rural buyers may need to travel to a dealer. The private gun market, including sellers who today move guns without any records, loses an unregulated channel. Gun-control opponents keep an issue to organize around either way.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private gun sellers and unregulated gun buyers

drawbacks.text: Every covered sale now costs the parties a dealer's processing fee and time, and buyers in rural areas may face long trips to the nearest licensed dealer. The bill sets no cap on these fees. [S3]

The bill only reaches transfers that happen through the legal market. Stolen guns, straw purchases made for prohibited buyers, and sales that simply go underground are unaffected, so it cannot stop every path a prohibited person has to a gun. [S3]
Enforcement depends on voluntary compliance by private parties; without broad registries or sales records, prosecutors may find it difficult to prove a private transfer occurred at all. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: checks on private sales screen out buyers with disqualifying records, which today they can avoid by buying from a stranger. The costs are real but modest — dealer fees and travel for rural buyers — and the bill's careful exemptions (family gifts, hunting loans, self-defense emergencies) answer most good-faith objections from gun owners. The honest limitation is that it cannot reach the illegal market; it raises the cost of buying a gun legally, not the difficulty of stealing one. On balance the bill is a targeted fix, not a sweeping restriction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on November 19, 2025, with 46 Senate cosponsors — 44 Democrats and 2 independents — and no Republican cosponsors listed. [S1][S4]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action has been taken. [S5]

Because it sits with no markup scheduled and no Republican cosponsors, the bill's path to a floor vote would require committee action and, in the Senate, 60 votes to move forward — support it does not currently have on the record. [S4][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, private sellers and opponents of expanded checks keep the current unregulated private-sale market; gun-control supporters have gained nothing yet.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Background Check Expansion Act and recruited 46 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 46 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors the day the bill was introduced, giving it a majority of the Senate on paper but no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (no chair listed in record)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 19, 2025 and has taken no action since.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, so the bill lacks the 60 votes any Senate bill needs to reach a final vote.

industries.note: The bill makes licensed dealers the mandatory channel for all private transfers, guaranteeing them a fee on every private sale in the country — a permanent new revenue stream written into law. Their gain comes attached to a public-safety purpose rather than against it.

industries.industry: Private firearms sellers and the secondary gun market
industries.note: The unregulated private-sale channel — no records, no checks, no fees — is closed. Anyone selling a gun outside the family exemptions must now route the sale through a dealer.

industries.industry: Gun owners and firearms retailers generally
industries.note: Gun owners face fees, paperwork, and travel for some transfers, but the bill's exemptions for family gifts, hunting loans, and range use keep most routine transfers untouched, and it explicitly bars a national gun registry.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to clear the Senate's 60-vote threshold or even get a Judiciary Committee markup this session. Barring a shift in Senate leadership's priorities or bipartisan outreach, it will most likely sit in committee until the Congress ends, as previous versions of this proposal have.
